senses.gloss:
avirati
(‘absence of renunciation’)
------------------------------------------
Patañjali (200 B. C.) the great teacher of योग, lists nine serious obstacles to the attainment of योग (vide Yogasūtras 1.30) of which ‘avirati’ or absence of the spirit of renunciation is one. योग is ‘citta-वृत्ति-nirodha’ or suppressing the modifications of the मिन्द्. These modifications continue to rise as long as their causes like काम or desire for the pleasures of the senses exist. काम has to be controlled by ‘virati’ or dispassion or an intense spirit of renunciation. If this virati is absent, then, that state is called ‘avirati’ which is a serious obstacle to योग.

Aviyoga-vrata
(‘religious vow for non-separation’)
------------------------------------------
Hinduism considers the ties of मर्रिअगे to be sacred and inviolable. A married Hindu woman shudders at the least prospect of separation from her husband. ‘Aviyoga-vrata’ (also called ‘Aviyoga-tṛtīyā’) is a religious vow specially prescribed for a married woman and is supposed to bring about non-separation from her husband. It begins on the 3rd day of the bright half of Mārgaśira (November-December) and continues for one year. The women who undertake this vrata start it on this day by partaking rice boiled in milk and sugar. They worship गौरी (Pārvatī) and Śambhu (Śiva) in images made of rice flour, under different names (in each of the twelve months) with different flowers.
See also VRATAS.

Avidhavā-navamī-śrāddha
(‘obsequial rites to a dead non-widow, on the ninth day’)
------------------------------------------
Married Hindu ladies cherish death before that of their husbands. Such ladies are called ‘avidhavās’ or ‘non-widows.’ The śrāddha or obsequial rite for such women is performed on the ninth day during the dark half of the month Bhādrapada (corresponding roughly to September) by their sons or younger male relatives. One of the specialities of this rite is that not only a ब्राह्मण but also married ladies whose husbands are alive, are invited, fed and given presents. The rite generally ceases to be performed when their husbands die.

avikṛta-परिणाम-vāda
(‘doctrine of unchanged transformation’)
------------------------------------------
Among the post-शङ्कर schools of Vedānta, the शुद्धाद्वैत (also known as ‘Puṣṭimārga’) of वल्लभ (A. D. 1473-1531) is an important one. This school based equally on the authority of the Bhagavadgītā and the Bhāgavata as also on the वेदस् and the Brahmasūtras, posits ब्रह्मन् as personal. He creates this world in ‘līlā’ or sport out of himself. But though this world is a ‘pariṇāma’ or a transformation of his, he continues to remain ‘avikṛta’ or unchanged, since the entire process is only a līlā. This doctrine is therefore called ‘avikṛta-परिणाम-वाद.’
See also PUṢṬIMĀRGA, ŚUDDHĀDVAITA and VALLABHĀCĀRYA.

avidyā
(‘non-knowledge’)
------------------------------------------
How ब्रह्मन्, ‘the One without a second,’ the only Reality, appears as this phenomenal universe, is a question that has baffled the Indian philosophers who have accepted the final authority of the śruti or the वेदस्, for ages. शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) posits अविद्या, अज्ञान or māyā as the factor responsible for this. (See AJÑĀNA for details.) Later Advaitins have tried to present māyā as the cause and अविद्या or अज्ञान as its effect. The latter words have been variously rendered as ‘nescience,’ ‘ignorance,’ ‘non-knowledge’ or even ‘anti-knowledge.’ In the final analysis it defies all definition.
The word ‘avidyā’ has been used by पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) in his Yogasūtras (2.3-5). He considers it as one of the five ‘kleśas’ or afflictions, but as the ground for the origin of the others. He defines it as that which makes us feel that the transient is eternal, the impure is pure, misery is happiness and the non-self is the Self. It can be eliminated only by ‘viveka-ख्याति’ the knowledge that we as the Self (which is pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्) are entirely separate and different from प्रकृति or insentient nature.
